name: Traps
entries: Traps should be used sparingly, lest they lose their charm. A hidden pit can be a fun surprise, but too many traps in an adventure can lead players to become overly cautious, which slows down the game.

The best traps are fleeting distractions that skilled characters can overcome in a short amount of time or deadly puzzles that require quick thinking and teamwork to overcome. Traps that are undetectable and inescapable are rarely fun.

entries.name: Parts of a Trap
entries: The description of a trap includes the following parts after the trap's name:

items.name: Severity and Levels
items.entry: A trap is designated as a nuisance or as deadly for characters of certain levels. A nuisance trap is unlikely to kill or seriously harm characters of the indicated levels, whereas a deadly trap can grievously damage characters of the indicated levels.

items.name: Trigger
items.entry: Traps are often set to go off when a creature enters an area or touches an object. Examples of triggers include stepping on a pressure plate, crossing a trip wire, turning a doorknob, or using the wrong key in a lock.

items.name: Duration
items.entry: Some traps have durations expressed in rounds, minutes, or hours. Others specify that their effects last until the trap is destroyed or dispelled. If a trap's duration is instantaneous, its effect is resolved instantly.

entries: Use caution when introducing a trap to characters of a level lower than the trap's level range. A trap that is a nuisance at one level range could be deadly to characters of a lower level range.

name: Stat Block Overview
entries: A monster has a stat block that contains the rules necessary to use it in the game. Stat blocks are divided into the following parts:

items.name: Name and General Details
items.entry: The name of the monster is followed by its size, creature type (along with any descriptive tags), and alignment.

items.name: Combat Highlights
items.entry: {@variantrule Armor Class|srd52}, {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52}, {@variantrule Speed|srd52}, and {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} are provided here.

items.name: Ability Scores
items.entry: A monster's ability scores, ability modifiers, and saving throws are listed here.

items.name: Other Details
items.entry: The monster's Senses, Languages, and CR entries appear here. Additional details appear in some monsters, such as skill proficiencies, Resistances, Immunities, and Gear. If a monster lacks those details, entries for them don't appear.

items.name: Traits
items.entry: Monster characteristics that are active at all times or during certain situations appear here.

items.name: Actions
items.entry: The monster can take the actions here in addition to those in "Playing the Game".

items.name: Bonus Actions
items.entry: This section provides a monster's Bonus Actions, if any.

items.name: Reactions and Legendary Actions
items.entry: These sections provide Reactions and Legendary Actions, if any.

name: Parts of a Stat Block
entries: The rules for a stat block are detailed in "Rules Glossary" and in this section.

entries.name: Size
entries: A monster is Tiny, Small, Medium, Large, Huge, or Gargantuan. If size options are presented, you choose the creature's size from those options. See "Playing the Game" for information on size.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: Each monster has a tag that identifies the type of creature it is. Certain spells, magic items, class features, and other effects in the game interact in special ways with creatures of a particular type.
The game includes the following creature types, which have no rules of their own:

items.name: Aberrations
items.entry: are utterly alien beings, such as aboleths and cloakers.

items.name: Beasts
items.entry: are non-Humanoid natural creatures, like horses and wolves, as well as most giant animals.

items.name: Celestials
items.entry: are magical creatures, such as angels and pegasi, with ties to the Upper Planes.

items.name: Constructs
items.entry: are magically created creatures such as homunculi and shield guardians.

items.name: Dragons
items.entry: are scaly beings of ancient origin, such as red dragons and wyverns.

items.name: Elementals
items.entry: are beings from the Elemental Planes, such as efreet and water elementals.

items.name: Fey
items.entry: are creatures tied to the Feywild or the forces of nature, such as dryads and goblins.

items.name: Fiends
items.entry: are creatures tied to terrifying Lower Planes, such as balors and hell hounds.

items.name: Giants
items.entry: are towering beings with humanlike shapes, like fire giants and trolls.

items.name: Humanoids
items.entry: are people defined by their roles and professions, such as mages, pirates, and warriors. They include members of varied species.

items.name: Monstrosities
items.entry: are unnatural creatures with strange origins, such as mimics and owlbears.

items.name: Oozes
items.entry: are gelatinous creatures, including black puddings and gelatinous cubes.

items.name: Plants
items.entry: are sentient vegetation and fungal monsters, such as shambling mounds and treants.

items.name: Undead
items.entry: are spirits and the reanimated dead, such as ghosts, vampires, and zombies.

entries.name: Descriptive Tags
entries: A monster might have one or more tags in parentheses following its type. Such tags provide additional categorization and have no rules of their own, but certain game effects might refer to them.

entries.name: Alignment
entries: The alignment specified in a monster's stat block is a default suggestion of how to roleplay the monster, inspired by its traditional role in the game or real-world folklore. Change a monster's alignment to suit your storytelling needs. The Neutral alignment, in particular, is an invitation for you to consider whether an individual leans toward one of the other alignments.
"Character Creation" describes the nine alignments and unaligned creatures.

entries.name: Armor Class
entries: A monster's {@variantrule Armor Class|srd52} (AC) includes its natural armor, Dexterity, gear, and other defenses. See "Playing the Game" for information on Armor Class.

entries.name: Initiative
entries: The {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} entry specifies the monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} modifier followed by the monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} score in parentheses. Use the modifier when you roll to determine a monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52}. A monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} modifier is typically equal to its Dexterity modifier, but some monsters have additional modifiers, such as {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus}, applied to that number.

If you don't want to roll a monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52}, use the {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} score as the monster's {@variantrule Initiative|srd52} in combat. Initiative is further detailed in "Playing the Game".

entries.name: Hit Points
entries: A monster's {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} are presented as a number followed by parentheses, where the monster's {@variantrule Hit Point Dice|srd52} are provided, along with any contribution from its Constitution. Either use the number for the monster's {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} or roll the die expression in parentheses to determine the monster's {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} randomly; don't use both.
A monster's size typically determines the die used to calculate its {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52}, as shown in the Hit Dice by {@variantrule Size|srd52} table.
See the Hit Dice by Size table.

A monster's Constitution modifier is multiplied by the number of Hit Dice it possesses, and the result is added to its {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52}. For example, if a monster has a Constitution of 12 (+1 modifier) and {@dice 2d8} Hit Dice, it has {@dice 2d8 + 2} {@variantrule Hit Points|srd52} (average 11).
For more on Hit Points, see "Playing the Game".

entries.name: Speed
entries: The Speed entry specifies a monster's Speed. Some monsters have one or more of the following speeds: {@variantrule Burrow Speed|srd52|Burrow}, {@variantrule Climb Speed|srd52|Climb}, {@variantrule Fly Speed|srd52|Fly}, {@variantrule Swim Speed|srd52|Swim}. Rules for Speed and these specials speeds appear in "Rules Glossary".

entries.name: Ability Scores
entries: Every monster has six ability scores along with corresponding ability score modifiers and saving throw modifiers. For more information on ability scores and saving throws, see "Playing the Game".

entries.name: Skills
entries: The Skills entry specifies a monster's skill proficiencies, if any. For example, a monster that is very perceptive and stealthy might have bonuses to Wisdom ({@skill Perception|srd52}) and Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|srd52}) checks. A skill bonus is the sum of a monster's relevant ability modifier and its {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus}. Other modifiers might apply.

entries.name: Resistances and Vulnerabilities
entries: These entries list a monster's Resistances and Vulnerabilities, if any. See "Playing the Game" for more information.

entries.name: Immunities
entries: This entry lists the monster's {@variantrule Immunity|srd52|Immunities}, if any. If the monster has damage and condition Immunities, the damage types are listed before the conditions. See "Playing the Game" for details.

entries.name: Gear
entries: Monsters have proficiency with their equipment. If a monster has equipment that can be given away or retrieved, the items are listed in the Gear entry. The monster's stat block might include special flourishes that happen when the monster uses an item, and the stat block might ignore the rules in "Equipment" for that item. When used by someone else, a retrievable item uses its "Equipment" rules, ignoring any special flourishes in the stat block.
The Gear entry doesn't necessarily list all of a monster's equipment. For example, a monster that wears clothes is assumed to be dressed appropriately, and those clothes aren't in this entry.
Equipment mentioned outside the Gear entry is considered to be supernatural or highly specialized, and it is unusable when the monster is defeated.

entries.name: Ammunition and Ranged Attacks
entries: A monster that requires ammunition to make ranged attacks carries the necessary ammunition.

entries.name: Equipping a Monster with Other Items
entries: You may equip monsters with additional gear however you like, using the items in "Equipment" for inspiration. You decide how much of a monster's equipment is recoverable after the creature is slain and whether any of that equipment is still usable.

Beware of giving a monster combat-oriented magic items, since those might alter the monster's {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52}. If you do give a monster a magic item, the monster can have {@variantrule Attunement|srd52} with magic items as noted in "Equipment". A monster with a class tag after its creature type is considered a member of that class for {@variantrule Attunement|srd52} purposes.

entries.name: Running a Monster
entries: To ensure a monster acts in accordance with its {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52}, follow these rules during combat:

items.name: Special Abilities
items.entry: If the monster has a special ability that deals a lot of damage but has a limited number of uses, such as a recharging breath weapon or a spell it can cast only once per day, have it use that special ability as quickly and as often as possible.

items.name: Multiattack
items.entry: If the monster has Multiattack, have it use Multiattack on any of its turns in which it's not using one of its more powerful abilities.

items.name: Bonus Actions, Reactions, Legendary Actions
items.entry: If the monster has Bonus Actions, Reactions, or Legendary Actions in its stat block, make sure it uses them as often as it can.

entries.name: Senses
entries: The Senses entry specifies a monster's {@variantrule Passive Perception|srd52} score, as well as any special senses the monster possesses. Passive Perception and special senses are described in "Rules Glossary".

entries.name: Languages
entries: This entry lists languages that the monster can use to communicate. Sometimes a monster can understand a language but can't communicate with it, which is noted in its entry. "None" indicates that a creature doesn't comprehend any language.

entries.name: Telepathy
entries: Telepathy is a magical ability that allows a creature to communicate mentally with another creature within a specified range. See "Rules Glossary" for more information.

entries.name: Challenge Rating
entries: Challenge Rating is defined in "Rules Glossary", while guidance on using CR to plan potential combat encounters is in "Gameplay Toolbox".

entries.name: Experience Points
entries: The number of {@variantrule Experience Points|srd52} (XP) a monster is worth is based on its CR, as detailed in the {@variantrule Experience Points|srd52} by {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52} table. XP is awarded for defeating the monster in combat or otherwise neutralizing it.
Unless a rule says otherwise, a monster summoned by a spell or another magical ability is worth the XP noted in its stat block.
See the Experience Points by Challenge Rating table.

entries.name: Proficiency Bonus
entries: A monster's {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus} (PB) is determined by its CR, as shown in the {@variantrule Proficiency|srd52|Proficiency Bonus} by {@variantrule Challenge Rating|srd52} table, and is reflected in saving throws, skills, and other statistics where the monster's exceptional aptitude is a factor.
See the Proficiency Bonus by Challenge Rating table.

entries.name: Traits
entries: A monster's traits, if any, are features that are active at all times or in certain situations.

entries.name: Actions
entries: A monster can take the actions in this section or take one of the actions available to all creatures, as described in "Playing the Game".

entries.name: Attack Notation
entries: The entry for a monster's attack identifies whether the attack is a melee or a ranged attack and then provides the attack roll's bonus, its reach or range, and what happens on a hit. An attack is against one target unless its entry says otherwise. For details on different kinds of attacks, see "Playing the Game" and "Spells".

entries.name: Hit
entries: Any damage dealt or other effects that occur as a result of an attack hitting a target are described after the "Hit:" notation.

entries.name: Miss
entries: If an attack has an effect that occurs on a miss, that information follows the "Miss:" notation.

entries.name: Hit or Miss
entries: If an attack has an effect that occurs regardless of whether it hits or misses its target, that information follows the "Hit or Miss:" notation.

entries.name: Saving Throw Effect Notation
entries: If an effect forces a saving throw, the effect identifies the kind of save required and then provides the save's DC, a description of which creatures make the save, and an explanation of what happens on a failed or successful save.
"Half damage only" on a successful save means the target takes half as much damage (round down) as targets that fail the save, while also ignoring all other parts of the effect.

entries.name: Damage Notation
entries: A stat block usually provides both a number and a die expression for each instance of damage. For example, an attack might deal 4 ({@damage 1d4 + 2}) damage on a hit. You decide whether to use the number or the die expression in parentheses; don't use both.

entries.name: Multiattack
entries: Some creatures can make more than one attack when they take the {@action Attack|srd52} action. Such creatures have the Multiattack entry in the "Actions" section of their stat block. This entry details the attacks a creature can make, as well as any additional abilities it can use, as part of the {@action Attack|srd52} action.

entries.name: Spellcasting
entries: If a monster can cast any spells, its stat block lists the spells and provides the monster's spellcasting ability, spell save DC (if any spells require a saving throw), and spell attack bonus (if any spells require an attack roll). Unless noted otherwise, a spell of level 1 or higher is always cast at its lowest possible level and can't be cast at a higher level.

A monster's spell can have special rules or restrictions. For example, a green hag can cast the {@spell Invisibility|srd52} spell, but the spell has a "self only" restriction, which means the spell affects only the hag.

entries.name: Spell Components
entries: The Spellcasting trait notes whether the monster's spellcasting ignores the need for certain spell components. If any spell components are required, describe the monster's use of Verbal, Somatic, or Material components to signal to characters that it is casting a spell. A monster that requires Material components has them.

entries.name: Casting Times of 1+ Minutes
entries: If a spell has a casting time of 1 minute or more yet is listed in a spellcasting action, the monster doesn't cast the spell in just one action unless the action's description states otherwise; the monster must take the {@action Magic|srd52} action on each of its turns and maintain {@status Concentration|srd52} to cast the spell, as described in "Rules Glossary".

entries.name: Bonus Action
entries: If a monster has Bonus Action options, they are listed in this section. See "Playing the Game" for details on Bonus Actions.

entries.name: Reactions
entries: If the monster has Reaction options, those are listed in this section along with their triggers. See "Playing the Game" for details on Reactions.

entries.name: Legendary Actions
entries: If the monster has Legendary Action options, those are listed in this section. A Legendary Action is an action that a monster can take immediately after another creature's turn. Only one of these actions can be taken at a time and only after another creature's turn ends. The monster can't take a Legendary Action if it has the {@condition Incapacitated|srd52} condition or is otherwise unable to take actions.

The monster has a limited number of Legendary Action uses, and that number is specified in the stat block. The monster expends one use whenever it takes a Legendary Action, and it regains all expended uses at the start of each of its turns.

entries.name: Limited Usage
entries: Some parts of a stat block have restrictions on the number of times they can be used. Here are the most common ways that usage is limited:

items.name: X/Day
entries: This notation means the stat block part can be used a certain number of times (represented by X) and that a monster must finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52} to regain expended uses. For example, a {@variantrule Reaction|srd52} that includes "1/Day" means the {@variantrule Reaction|srd52} can be taken once and that the monster must finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52} to take it again.

items.name: Recharge X–Y
entries: This notation means a monster can use the stat block part once. At the start of each of the monster's turns, roll {@dice 1d6}. If the roll is within the number range given in the notation (represented by X–Y), the monster regains the use of that part, which also recharges when the monster finishes a {@variantrule Short Rest|srd52|Short} or {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52}. For example, "Recharge 5–6" in an action means a monster can take the action once. Then, at the start of each of the monster's turns, it regains the use of that action if it rolls a 5 or 6 on {@dice 1d6}.

items.name: Recharge after a Short or Long Rest
entries: This notation means the monster can use the stat block part once and must then finish a {@variantrule Short Rest|srd52|Short} or {@variantrule Long Rest|srd52} to use it again.

name: Weapons
entries: The Weapons table in this section shows the game's main weapons. The table lists the cost and weight of each weapon, as well as the following details:

items.name: Category
items.entry: Every weapon falls into a category: Simple or Martial. Weapon proficiencies are usually tied to one of these categories. For example, you might have proficiency with Simple weapons.

items.name: Melee or Ranged
items.entry: A weapon is classified as either Melee or Ranged. A Melee weapon is used to attack a target within 5 feet, whereas a Ranged weapon is used to attack at a greater distance.

items.name: Damage
items.entry: The table lists the amount of damage a weapon deals when an attacker hits with it as well as the type of that damage.

items.name: Properties
items.entry: Any properties a weapon has are listed in the Properties column. Each property is defined in the "Properties" section.

items.name: Mastery
items.entry: Each weapon has a mastery property, which is defined in the "Mastery Properties" section. To use that property, you must have a feature that lets you use it.

entries: See the Weapons table.

entries.name: Weapon Proficiency
entries: Anyone can wield a weapon, but you must have proficiency with it to add your Proficiency Bonus to an attack roll you make with it. A player character's features can provide weapon proficiencies. A monster is proficient with any weapon in its stat block.

entries.name: Range
entries: A Range weapon has a range in parentheses after the {@itemProperty A|srd52|Ammunition} or {@itemProperty T|srd52|Thrown} property. The range lists two numbers. The first is the weapon's normal range in feet, and the second is the weapon's long range. When attacking a target beyond normal range, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on the attack roll. You can't attack a target beyond the long range.

entries.name: Thrown

entries.name: Two-Handed
entries: See Two-Handed.

entries.name: Versatile

entries.name: Improvised Weapons
entries: If you use an object—such as a table leg, frying pan, or bottle—as a makeshift weapon, see "{@variantrule Improvised Weapons|srd52}" in the rules glossary. Also see those rules if you wield a weapon in an unusual way, such as using a Ranged weapon to make a melee attack.

entries.name: Mastery Properties
entries: Each weapon has a mastery property, which is usable only by a character who has a feature, such as Weapon Mastery, that unlocks the property for the character. See Mastery Properties.
See the canonical Mastery Properties rule and individual mastery definitions.

name: Armor
entries: The Armor table lists the game's main armor. The table includes the cost and weight of armor, as well as the following details:

items.name: Category
items.entry: Every type of armor falls into a category: Light, Medium, or Heavy. The category determines how long it takes to don or doff the armor (as shown in the table).

entries: {@b Armor Class (AC)}. The table's Armor Class column tells you what your base AC is when you wear a type of armor. For example, if you wear Leather Armor, your base AC is 11 plus your Dexterity modifier, whereas your AC is 16 in Chain Mail.

items.name: Strength
items.entry: If the table shows a Strength score in the Strength column for an armor type, that armor reduces the wearer's speed by 10 feet unless the wearer has a Strength score equal to or higher than the listed score.

items.name: Stealth
items.entry: If the table shows "Disadvantage" in the Stealth column for an armor type, the wearer has {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on Dexterity ({@skill Stealth|srd52}) checks.

entries: See the Armor table.

entries.name: Armor Training
entries: Anyone can don armor or hold a Shield, but only those with training can use them effectively, as explained below. A character's class and other features determine the character's armor training. A monster has training with any armor in its stat block.

entries.name: Light, Medium, or Heavy Armor
entries: If you wear Light, Medium, or Heavy armor and lack training with it, you have {@variantrule Disadvantage|srd52} on any {@variantrule D20 Test|srd52} that involves Strength or Dexterity, and you can't cast spells.

entries.name: Shield
entries: You gain the Armor Class benefit of a Shield only if you have training with it.

entries.name: One at a Time
entries: A creature can wear only one suit of armor at a time and wield only one Shield at a time.

name: Tools
entries: A tool helps you make specialized ability checks, craft certain items, or both. A tool's description includes the tool's cost and weight, as well as the following entries:

items.name: Ability
items.entry: This entry lists the ability to use when making an ability check with the tool.

items.name: Utilize
items.entry: This entry lists things you can do with the tool when you take the {@action Utilize|srd52} action. You can do one of those things each time you take the action. This entry also provides the DC for the action.

items.name: Craft
items.entry: This entry lists what, if anything, you can craft with the tool. For crafting rules, see "Crafting Nonmagical Items," "Brewing Potions of Healing," and "Scribing Spell Scrolls" later in "Equipment".

items.name: Variants
items.entry: This entry appears if the tool has variants, which are listed. Each requires a separate proficiency.

entries.name: Tool Proficiency
entries: If you have proficiency with a tool, add your Proficiency Bonus to any ability check you make that uses the tool. If you have proficiency in a skill that's used with that check, you have {@variantrule Advantage|srd52} on the check too.
Your features might give you proficiency with a tool. A monster has proficiency with any tool in its stat block.

name: Character Backgrounds
entries: Your character's background is a collection of characteristics that represent the place and occupation that were most formative before your character embarked on a life of adventure.

entries.name: Parts of a Background
entries: A background includes the following parts.

entries.name: Ability Scores
entries: A background lists three of your character's ability scores. Increase one by 2 and another one by 1, or increase all three by 1. None of these increases can raise a score above 20.

entries.name: Feat
entries: A background gives your character a specified Origin feat (described in Feats).

entries.name: Skill Proficiencies
entries: A background gives your character proficiency in two specified skills.

entries.name: Tool Proficiency
entries: Each background gives a character proficiency with one tool—either a specific tool or one chosen from the Artisan's Tools category. Tools are detailed in "Equipment".

entries.name: Equipment
entries: Each background offers a choice between a package of equipment and 50 GP.

name: Character Species
entries: When you choose your character's species, you determine whether your character is a human or a member of a fantastical species, such as dragonborn or gnome.

The peoples of the multiverse hail from different worlds and include many kinds of sapient life forms. A player character's species is the set of game traits that an adventurer gains from being one of those life forms.

Some species can trace their origin to a single world, plane of existence, or god, while other species first appeared in multiple realms at once. Whatever a species' genesis, its members have spread across the multiverse and contribute to many different cultures.

Members of most species live for about 80 years, with exceptions noted in the text about the species in "Character Origins". Regardless of life span, members of all species reach physical maturity at about the same age. Your character can be any age that isn't beyond their species' normal life span.

entries.name: Parts of a Species
entries: A species includes the following parts.

entries.name: Creature Type
entries: A character's species determines the character's creature type, which is described in the Rules Glossary. Every species in "Character Origins" is Humanoid; playable non-Humanoid species appear in other books.

entries.name: Size
entries: Your character's species determines the character's size. Individuals within a species cover a wide range of heights, and some species include such diversity of size that you can choose whether your character is Small or Medium.

entries.name: Speed
entries: Your character's species determines the character's Speed.

entries.name: Special Traits
entries: Each species gives a character special traits—unique characteristics based on the species' physiology or magical nature. When you choose a species, your character gets all the special traits listed for it. Some traits involve making a choice from a handful of options.

name: Feat Descriptions
entries: The feats that follow are organized by category— Origin, General, Fighting Style, or Epic Boon—and alphabetized in each category.

entries.name: Parts of a Feat
entries: The description of a feat contains the following parts, which are presented after the feat's name.

entries.name: Category
entries: A feat is a member of a category, which is noted in the feat. If you're instructed to choose a feat from a specific category, such as the Origin category, that category must appear under the feat's name. If you're instructed to choose a feat and no category is specified, you can choose from any category.

entries.name: Prerequisite
entries: To take a feat, you must meet any prerequisite in its description unless a feature allows you to take the feat without the prerequisite. If a prerequisite includes a class, you must have at least 1 level in that class to take the feat.

entries.name: Benefit
entries: The benefits of a feat are detailed after any prerequisites are listed. If you have a feat, you gain its benefits.

entries.name: Repeatable
entries: A feat can be taken only once unless its description states otherwise in a "Repeatable" subsection.

name: Glossary Conventions
entries: The glossary uses the following conventions:

items.name: Tags in Brackets
items.entry: Some entries have a tag in brackets after the entry's name, as in "Attack [Action]." A tag—Action, Area of Effect, Attitude, Condition, or Hazard—indicates that a rule is part of a family of rules. The tags also have glossary entries.

items.name: "You"
items.entry: The game's rules—in this glossary and elsewhere—often talk about something happening to you in the game world. That "you" refers to the creature or object that the rule applies to in a particular moment of play. For example, the "you" in the {@condition Prone|srd52} condition is a creature that currently has that condition.

items.name: "See Also"
items.entry: Some glossary entries include a See also section that points to other entries in the glossary, to other parts of this document, or both.

items.name: No Obsolete Terms
items.entry: The glossary contains definitions of current rules terms only. If you're looking for a term from an earlier version of the fifth edition rules, consult the index.

items.name: Abbreviations
items.entry: The abbreviations listed below appear in this glossary and elsewhere in the rules.
